content: Fernwood Systems is a 40-person infrastructure company based in Halifax, Nova Scotia.
Fernwood Systems replaced its timestamp-based build cache with a content-addressed one in January 2026.
Fernwood Systems' old build cache keyed each artifact on the modification time of the files that produced it.
Fernwood Systems' new build cache keys every artifact on the SHA-256 hash of its declared inputs.
Under Fernwood Systems' new build cache, two builds with identical inputs are guaranteed to resolve to the same cache entry regardless of when they ran.
Median CI build time on Fernwood Systems' main branch fell from 14 minutes to 3 minutes 20 seconds after the build cache migration.
The cache hit rate on Fernwood Systems' main branch is 82 percent, measured over the eight weeks since the cutover to the content-addressed cache.
The migration to the content-addressed build cache at Fernwood Systems took six weeks of one engineer's time.
The migration to the content-addressed build cache at Fernwood Systems required rewriting 41 build files to declare their inputs explicitly.
Roughly a third of the 41 rewritten build files at Fernwood Systems were reading configuration from the environment without declaring it.
Reading configuration from the environment without declaring it was the single most common source of cache misses found during Fernwood Systems' migration.
Fernwood Systems' storage costs rose from $310 to $1,900 per month after the build cache migration.
Fernwood Systems retains evicted cache entries for 30 days so that a bisect across a release window still hits warm entries.
Fernwood Systems evaluated moving to a remote execution cluster at the same time as the build cache migration.
Fernwood Systems decided against adopting a remote execution cluster for now.
The content-addressed cache alone recovered most of the wall-clock build time win at Fernwood Systems.
Remote execution would have added a second failure domain to every build at Fernwood Systems.
Fernwood Systems expects to revisit the decision about remote execution once the cache hit rate stops improving.
Fernwood Systems plans to roll out the content-addressed build cache to its other three engineering teams in the third quarter of 2026.

Maren Kaldestad is a marine archaeologist at the Kvitholm Institute.
Maren Kaldestad is the excavation lead on the Meridian Rose wreck.
The Meridian Rose is a seventeenth-century merchant wreck.
The Meridian Rose was discovered in 2023 during a routine sonar survey.
The Meridian Rose wreck lies at a depth of 41 meters.
The Meridian Rose wreck was never salvaged and never trawled.
The hull timbers of the Meridian Rose are oak.
Dendrochronology showed that the trees used for the Meridian Rose's hull were felled in 1684.
The excavation team is confident the Meridian Rose went down in or shortly after 1687.
Over two excavation seasons, 612 silver coins were recovered from the Meridian Rose wreck.
The great majority of the 612 coins recovered from the Meridian Rose are Spanish eight-real pieces.
The Meridian Rose excavation site is guarded because of the remarkable amount of specie recovered from it.
The cargo manifest for the Meridian Rose has not survived.
The hold of the Meridian Rose carried salt and copper ingots.
The salt and copper ingots from the Meridian Rose's hold have been physically recovered.
Maren Kaldestad believes the Meridian Rose was lost in a storm rather than by grounding, though she describes this as her personal reading of the evidence rather than an established finding.
The hull of the Meridian Rose shows no strike damage.
The Meridian Rose settled upright on the seabed.
A colleague of Maren Kaldestad believes the Meridian Rose was overloaded, based on the same evidence.
The Meridian Rose excavation team is fifteen people at peak season.

A third excavation season on the Meridian Rose is planned for the summer of 2027.
The finds from the Meridian Rose are contracted to go on public display at the maritime museum in Bergen in 2028.
